question.text: Why is night driving harder than daytime driving?

answer.text: Night driving is always harder and more hazardous than daytime driving because you see less, later and not as far, and oncoming headlight glare adds to the difficulty.

teaching.text: Darkness means you see less, later and not as far, and the glare of oncoming headlights makes it harder still. Remember: see less, later, shorter.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Night driving is always harder and more hazardous than daytime driving because you see less, later and not as far, and oncoming headlight glare adds to the difficulty.

question.text: How should you control your speed at night?

answer.text: At night, always be able to stop within the distance your headlights light up, and keep your speed under control and within posted limits.

teaching.text: Drive slowly enough to stop within the stretch of road your headlights light up, and stay within posted limits. Remember: stop within your lights.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At night, always be able to stop within the distance your headlights light up, and keep your speed under control and within posted limits.

question.text: Where should you look when oncoming headlights glare?

answer.text: Do not look straight into oncoming headlights; look down toward the right side of your lane, using the edge line or center line as a guide.

teaching.text: Turn your eyes away from oncoming headlights, down toward the right side of your lane, and use the lane lines as a guide. Remember: look down and right.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Do not look straight into oncoming headlights; look down toward the right side of your lane, using the edge line or center line as a guide.

question.text: What two night-driving rules cover sunglasses and the windshield?

answer.text: Never wear sunglasses when driving at night, and keep the windshield clean inside and out.

teaching.text: Sunglasses never belong on a night drive, and the windshield should be clean inside and out. Remember: no shades, clean glass.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never wear sunglasses when driving at night, and keep the windshield clean inside and out.

question.text: Why should you watch especially for pedestrians at night?

answer.text: Pedestrians are hard to see at night, so stay especially watchful for them after dark.

teaching.text: Pedestrians are hard to see at night, so give them extra attention after dark. Remember: walkers vanish after dark.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Pedestrians are hard to see at night, so stay especially watchful for them after dark.

question.text: What does the handbook report about fatal crashes in the early evening?

answer.text: Between two thousand fifteen and two thousand nineteen Nevada recorded two hundred seventy-six fatal crashes from six PM to eight fifty-nine PM, which was nineteen percent of all fatal crashes.

teaching.text: The handbook reports that between twenty fifteen and twenty nineteen, nineteen percent of Nevada's fatal crashes came in the early evening hours. Remember: evening hours turn deadly.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Between two thousand fifteen and two thousand nineteen Nevada recorded two hundred seventy-six fatal crashes from six PM to eight fifty-nine PM, which was nineteen percent of all fatal crashes.

question.text: When are headlights required by law?

answer.text: Headlights are required by law from a half hour after sunset to a half hour before sunrise, whenever there is not enough light, and whenever people or vehicles cannot be seen clearly at one thousand feet.

teaching.text: Headlights go on from a half hour after sunset to a half hour before sunrise, in low light, and when you cannot see clearly at one thousand feet. Remember: half hour after sunset.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Headlights are required by law from a half hour after sunset to a half hour before sunrise, whenever there is not enough light, and whenever people or vehicles cannot be seen clearly at one thousand feet.

question.text: When else are headlights required or advisable?

answer.text: Headlights are also required when an official traffic control device directs you to use them, and using them in rain, snow or fog is advisable.

teaching.text: Turn headlights on when a traffic control device says so, and it is wise to use them in rain, snow or fog. Remember: signs say, weather suggests.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Headlights are also required when an official traffic control device directs you to use them, and using them in rain, snow or fog is advisable.

question.text: When must you switch from high beams to low beams?

answer.text: Use high beams in open country at night, but switch to low beams at least five hundred feet before meeting an oncoming vehicle and three hundred feet before reaching a vehicle you are following.

teaching.text: High beams are for open country, and you dim them at least five hundred feet before oncoming cars and three hundred feet behind cars you follow. Remember: dim before meeting or following.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Use high beams in open country at night, but switch to low beams at least five hundred feet before meeting an oncoming vehicle and three hundred feet before reaching a vehicle you are following.

question.text: How far ahead must you dim for oncoming and for followed vehicles?

answer.text: High beams belong in open country at night, but you must dim to low beams at least five hundred feet before an oncoming vehicle and at least three hundred feet behind a vehicle you follow.

teaching.text: Five hundred feet for oncoming traffic and three hundred feet for the car ahead are the two dimming distances. Remember: five hundred, three hundred.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: High beams belong in open country at night, but you must dim to low beams at least five hundred feet before an oncoming vehicle and at least three hundred feet behind a vehicle you follow.

question.text: May you drive with only your parking lights on?

answer.text: Do not drive with only the parking lights on; you may flash your headlights to warn a driver ahead that you plan to pass.

teaching.text: Never drive on parking lights alone, though a quick flash of the headlights can warn a driver ahead that you plan to pass. Remember: parking lights never alone.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Do not drive with only the parking lights on; you may flash your headlights to warn a driver ahead that you plan to pass.

question.text: What is the most important thing to do in bad weather?

answer.text: The most important thing in bad weather is to slow down, since stopping distances on slippery roads can be two to ten times longer than on dry pavement.

teaching.text: Bad weather calls for slowing down first, since slippery stopping distances can run two to ten times longer. Remember: slow down first.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The most important thing in bad weather is to slow down, since stopping distances on slippery roads can be two to ten times longer than on dry pavement.

question.text: Why should you leave extra space in fog, rain or snow?

answer.text: Nevada weather can change suddenly with wind, rain and snowstorms, and in fog, rain or snow other drivers struggle to see just as you do, so leave extra space and watch the tail lights ahead.

teaching.text: In fog, rain or snow other drivers see as poorly as you, so add space and watch the tail lights ahead. Remember: others can't see either.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Nevada weather can change suddenly with wind, rain and snowstorms, and in fog, rain or snow other drivers struggle to see just as you do, so leave extra space and watch the tail lights ahead.

question.text: What equipment helps on snow and ice, and can equipped cars still slide?

answer.text: For snowy or icy roads, fit chains, snow tires or all-weather radials, and remember that even well-equipped vehicles can slide.

teaching.text: Chains, snow tires or all-weather radials help on ice and snow, but even well-equipped cars can slide. Remember: chains help, slides happen.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: For snowy or icy roads, fit chains, snow tires or all-weather radials, and remember that even well-equipped vehicles can slide.

question.text: How should you start and test your brakes on snow or ice?

answer.text: On snow or ice, start very slowly, test your brakes gently to learn how well you can stop, and begin slowing well before intersections and turns.

teaching.text: Start very slowly on snow or ice, test your brakes gently, and begin slowing long before turns and intersections. Remember: start slow, test brakes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On snow or ice, start very slowly, test your brakes gently to learn how well you can stop, and begin slowing well before intersections and turns.

question.text: Is any speed completely safe on snow and ice?

answer.text: No speed is completely safe on snow and ice, because conditions change with sun, shade and sanding from one block or stretch of road to the next.

teaching.text: There is no completely safe speed on snow and ice, because sun, shade and sanding change the road block by block. Remember: no speed is safe.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: No speed is completely safe on snow and ice, because conditions change with sun, shade and sanding from one block or stretch of road to the next.

question.text: How do you brake on slippery roads with and without ABS?

answer.text: On slippery roads, gentle braking with a slow, light touch-and-release pattern helps you stop safely, but a vehicle with ABS needs firm, continuous pedal pressure for the anti-lock feature to work.

teaching.text: Without ABS, brake gently with touch and release; with ABS, keep firm, continuous pressure so the system can work. Remember: tap without, press with.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On slippery roads, gentle braking with a slow, light touch-and-release pattern helps you stop safely, but a vehicle with ABS needs firm, continuous pedal pressure for the anti-lock feature to work.

question.text: How does braking on ice differ with ABS and without it?

answer.text: Without ABS, brake on ice with a slow, light touch-and-release pattern, while with ABS you hold firm, continuous pressure on the pedal; check the owner's manual.

teaching.text: The two braking methods are opposites: light touch and release without ABS, steady firm pressure with ABS. Remember: pulse versus steady press.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Without ABS, brake on ice with a slow, light touch-and-release pattern, while with ABS you hold firm, continuous pressure on the pedal; check the owner's manual.

question.text: What three habits help on snow and ice?

answer.text: On snow and ice avoid sudden changes in speed or direction, keep windows and windshield clear, and allow extra time to reach your destination.

teaching.text: On snow and ice, avoid sudden changes in speed or direction, keep the windows clear, and give yourself extra time. Remember: smooth, clear, extra time.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On snow and ice avoid sudden changes in speed or direction, keep windows and windshield clear, and allow extra time to reach your destination.

question.text: When may studded snow tires be used?

answer.text: Studded snow tires may be used only from October one through April thirty; tires with retractable studs are legal all year, but the studs may be engaged only within those dates.

teaching.text: Studded snow tires are allowed only from October one through April thirty, and retractable studs may be used only in those dates. Remember: October through April.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Studded snow tires may be used only from October one through April thirty; tires with retractable studs are legal all year, but the studs may be engaged only within those dates.

question.text: What is skidding, and where does it happen?

answer.text: Skidding means the tires have lost traction; it happens most on ice or packed snow but also on wet pavement or gravel.

teaching.text: A skid means the tires have lost their grip, most often on ice or packed snow but also on wet pavement or gravel. Remember: tires lose traction.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Skidding means the tires have lost traction; it happens most on ice or packed snow but also on wet pavement or gravel.

question.text: Where do you learn skid recovery for your own vehicle?

answer.text: Skid recovery differs by braking and steering system and by four-wheel or front-wheel drive, so the owner's manual is the source for your vehicle, and in any emergency stay calm.

teaching.text: Skid recovery depends on your car's braking, steering and drive system, so the owner's manual is the guide; stay calm. Remember: owner's manual, stay calm.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Skid recovery differs by braking and steering system and by four-wheel or front-wheel drive, so the owner's manual is the source for your vehicle, and in any emergency stay calm.

question.text: What should you do if your brakes fail?

answer.text: If the brakes fail, pump the pedal; if they still do not respond, use the parking brake and shift to a lower gear if possible, but never shift into park.

teaching.text: When brakes fail, pump them first, then use the parking brake and a lower gear, but never shift into park. Remember: pump, park brake, downshift.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If the brakes fail, pump the pedal; if they still do not respond, use the parking brake and shift to a lower gear if possible, but never shift into park.

question.text: Why use a lower gear on long downhill stretches?

answer.text: Use a lower gear when driving downhill for long stretches to avoid wearing out the brakes.

teaching.text: A lower gear on long downhill stretches keeps the brakes from wearing out. Remember: low gear saves brakes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Use a lower gear when driving downhill for long stretches to avoid wearing out the brakes.

question.text: What should you do if the gas pedal sticks?

answer.text: If the gas pedal sticks, quickly press it hard and release; if it stays stuck, shift to neutral, brake, and pull off to the right and stop, never shifting into park.

teaching.text: For a stuck gas pedal, tap it hard; if it stays stuck, shift to neutral, brake, and pull off to the right without shifting into park. Remember: tap, neutral, brake, pull off.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If the gas pedal sticks, quickly press it hard and release; if it stays stuck, shift to neutral, brake, and pull off to the right and stop, never shifting into park.

question.text: How do the steps differ for failed brakes and a stuck gas pedal?

answer.text: With failed brakes you shift to a lower gear and use the parking brake, while with a stuck gas pedal you shift to neutral and brake; in neither case do you shift into park.

teaching.text: Failed brakes call for a lower gear and the parking brake; a stuck pedal calls for neutral and braking; neither calls for park. Remember: lower gear versus neutral.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: With failed brakes you shift to a lower gear and use the parking brake, while with a stuck gas pedal you shift to neutral and brake; in neither case do you shift into park.

question.text: How do you test and dry brakes after deep water?

answer.text: After driving through deep water, test your brakes; dry them by driving slowly in low gear while braking lightly, testing about every two hundred feet until they work normally.

teaching.text: After deep water, test the brakes and dry them by driving slowly in low gear with light braking, checking about every two hundred feet. Remember: low gear, light braking.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: After driving through deep water, test your brakes; dry them by driving slowly in low gear while braking lightly, testing about every two hundred feet until they work normally.

question.text: What should you do if the wipers fail in heavy rain or snow?

answer.text: When the wipers stop working during heavy rain or snow, reduce speed, roll the window down and lean out to see, and get off the highway to the right and stop as soon as you can.

teaching.text: If the wipers quit in heavy rain or snow, slow down, roll the window down to see, and get off the highway to the right. Remember: window down, pull off.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When the wipers stop working during heavy rain or snow, reduce speed, roll the window down and lean out to see, and get off the highway to the right and stop as soon as you can.

question.text: What should you do if your headlights fail?

answer.text: If the headlights fail, slow down and leave the roadway as soon as possible, using parking lights, turn signals or four-way flashers, which usually still work, to guide you.

teaching.text: If the headlights fail, slow down and leave the road using parking lights, turn signals or flashers, which usually still work. Remember: flashers guide you off.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If the headlights fail, slow down and leave the roadway as soon as possible, using parking lights, turn signals or four-way flashers, which usually still work, to guide you.

question.text: What should you do when smoke comes from the engine area?

answer.text: If you see smoke rising from the engine area, slow, get off the road and shut off the ignition immediately, and open the hood with extreme caution.

teaching.text: Smoke from the engine means slow down, get off the road, shut off the ignition and open the hood with extreme caution. Remember: pull off, ignition off.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If you see smoke rising from the engine area, slow, get off the road and shut off the ignition immediately, and open the hood with extreme caution.

question.text: How do you deal with a vehicle fire?

answer.text: Never use water on a vehicle fire, because burning gasoline floats and spreads; use a chemical extinguisher or sand or dirt, and if the fire cannot be stopped move at least one hundred feet away.

teaching.text: Water spreads a gasoline fire, so use an extinguisher, sand or dirt, and move at least one hundred feet away if it cannot be stopped. Remember: no water on fire.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never use water on a vehicle fire, because burning gasoline floats and spreads; use a chemical extinguisher or sand or dirt, and if the fire cannot be stopped move at least one hundred feet away.

question.text: What should you do if the steering fails?

answer.text: If steering fails, ease off the accelerator; if the car holds its lane, slow and brake gently with flashers on, but brake hard if it heads off the road or toward a vehicle or pedestrian.

teaching.text: When steering fails, ease off the gas; brake gently with flashers if the car holds its lane, or hard if it heads off the road or toward someone. Remember: ease off, brake carefully.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If steering fails, ease off the accelerator; if the car holds its lane, slow and brake gently with flashers on, but brake hard if it heads off the road or toward a vehicle or pedestrian.

question.text: What should you do if a vehicle comes at you in your lane?

answer.text: If a vehicle comes at you in your lane, slow down, sound the horn, flash your headlights and pull as far right as is safe, without swerving into the lane it left.

teaching.text: For a car coming at you in your lane, slow down, sound the horn, flash your lights and pull right, never into the lane it left. Remember: slow, honk, go right.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If a vehicle comes at you in your lane, slow down, sound the horn, flash your headlights and pull as far right as is safe, without swerving into the lane it left.

question.text: What makes run-off-road crashes so serious in Nevada?

answer.text: Running off the road causes serious single-vehicle crashes that account for many Nevada deaths, with fatigue, inattention and speeding as major factors.

teaching.text: Run-off-road crashes are serious single-vehicle crashes behind many Nevada deaths, driven by fatigue, inattention and speeding. Remember: fatigue, distraction, speed kill.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Running off the road causes serious single-vehicle crashes that account for many Nevada deaths, with fatigue, inattention and speeding as major factors.

question.text: How should you recover after drifting onto the shoulder?

answer.text: If you drift onto the shoulder, stay calm, lift off the gas, brake only carefully, grip the wheel firmly, and do not swerve back; stay on the shoulder until fully in control, then ease back onto the road.

teaching.text: After drifting onto the shoulder, stay calm, lift off the gas, brake carefully, hold the wheel firmly, and ease back only when in control. Remember: stay on, then ease back.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If you drift onto the shoulder, stay calm, lift off the gas, brake only carefully, grip the wheel firmly, and do not swerve back; stay on the shoulder until fully in control, then ease back onto the road.

question.text: What should you do in a tire blowout?

answer.text: In a tire blowout, grip the wheel firmly and ease off the gas without hitting the brakes, then brake gently only once the vehicle is under control and has slowed.

teaching.text: In a blowout, hold the wheel firmly and ease off the gas without braking, and brake gently only once the car is under control. Remember: grip, ease off, no brakes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In a tire blowout, grip the wheel firmly and ease off the gas without hitting the brakes, then brake gently only once the vehicle is under control and has slowed.

question.text: How does braking differ after a blowout and after a shoulder drift?

answer.text: In a blowout you must not hit the brakes until the vehicle is under control, whereas after drifting onto the shoulder you may brake, but only carefully; in both cases grip the wheel firmly and lift off the gas.

teaching.text: A blowout means no brakes until you are in control; a shoulder drift allows careful braking; both mean a firm grip and no gas. Remember: blowout no brake, drift careful.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In a blowout you must not hit the brakes until the vehicle is under control, whereas after drifting onto the shoulder you may brake, but only carefully; in both cases grip the wheel firmly and lift off the gas.

question.text: What should you do once a blowout is under control?

answer.text: After a blowout, signal, pull safely off the road and warn others with parking lights or flashers.

teaching.text: Once a blowout is under control, signal, pull safely off the road and warn others with parking lights or flashers. Remember: signal, pull off, warn.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: After a blowout, signal, pull safely off the road and warn others with parking lights or flashers.

question.text: What should you do with a disabled vehicle?

answer.text: With a disabled vehicle, get all four wheels off the roadway if possible, warn other drivers with parking lights, flashers or flares, and have it towed as soon as you can.

teaching.text: A disabled car belongs fully off the roadway if possible, with lights, flashers or flares warning others until it is towed. Remember: off road, warn, tow.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: With a disabled vehicle, get all four wheels off the roadway if possible, warn other drivers with parking lights, flashers or flares, and have it towed as soon as you can.

question.text: Why are flash floods a risk in Nevada?

answer.text: Nevada's dry climate makes flash floods likely, especially in summer storms, spring thaw or long rains, and floating vehicles drift toward deeper, faster water where top-heavy ones may roll.

teaching.text: Nevada's dry climate makes flash floods likely in summer storms, spring thaw or long rains, and floating cars drift toward deeper water. Remember: dry land floods fast.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Nevada's dry climate makes flash floods likely, especially in summer storms, spring thaw or long rains, and floating vehicles drift toward deeper, faster water where top-heavy ones may roll.

question.text: How dangerous is shallow water for vehicles?

answer.text: More than half of all flash flood deaths involve vehicles, and less than one inch of water can make a driver lose control.

teaching.text: More than half of flash flood deaths involve vehicles, and less than one inch of water can take away a driver's control. Remember: an inch can matter.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: More than half of all flash flood deaths involve vehicles, and less than one inch of water can make a driver lose control.

question.text: How much water can float a vehicle or push it off the road?

answer.text: Most vehicles can float in two feet of water or less, and a car moving fast can be pushed off the road by only six inches of water.

teaching.text: Two feet of water can float most vehicles, and just six inches can push a fast-moving car off the road. Remember: two feet floats cars.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Most vehicles can float in two feet of water or less, and a car moving fast can be pushed off the road by only six inches of water.

question.text: Why should you never drive through a flooded road?

answer.text: Never try to drive through a flooded road; turn around and take another route or wait for the water to go down, since its depth and whether the road beneath has washed out cannot be judged.

teaching.text: Never drive into a flooded road; you cannot judge the depth or whether the road beneath has washed away, so turn around or wait. Remember: turn around, don't guess.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never try to drive through a flooded road; turn around and take another route or wait for the water to go down, since its depth and whether the road beneath has washed out cannot be judged.

question.text: What should you do if your vehicle stalls in rising water?

answer.text: If your vehicle stalls in rising flood water and it is safe, leave it at once and get to higher ground.

teaching.text: If your car stalls in rising water and it is safe to do so, get out right away and head for higher ground. Remember: leave it, climb higher.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If your vehicle stalls in rising flood water and it is safe, leave it at once and get to higher ground.

question.text: What is the only sure flood safety rule?

answer.text: The only sure flood safety rule is to turn around and stay off flooded roads, and you must never drive around barricades that officials have put up.

teaching.text: Turning around is the only sure flood rule, and barricades put up by officials are never to be driven around. Remember: turn around, respect barricades.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The only sure flood safety rule is to turn around and stay off flooded roads, and you must never drive around barricades that officials have put up.

question.text: What extra flood cautions apply at night and near flowing water?

answer.text: Be extra careful about floods at night, never cross flowing streams or water over the road, and when water rises fast turn around and move to higher ground away from creeks and flood channels.

teaching.text: Floods are harder to spot at night, flowing water over a road should never be crossed, and rising water means turn back and climb higher. Remember: never cross flowing water.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Be extra careful about floods at night, never cross flowing streams or water over the road, and when water rises fast turn around and move to higher ground away from creeks and flood channels.

question.text: How are work zones marked, and what should you expect in them?

answer.text: Work zones are marked with orange signs, cones and barrels; lanes narrow, surfaces are rough and traffic may stop completely, so stay alert and expect stopped cars ahead.

teaching.text: Orange signs, cones and barrels mark work zones, where lanes narrow, surfaces get rough and traffic can stop completely. Remember: orange means stopped traffic.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Work zones are marked with orange signs, cones and barrels; lanes narrow, surfaces are rough and traffic may stop completely, so stay alert and expect stopped cars ahead.

question.text: What happens if you move barriers to drive onto a closed road?

answer.text: Moving barriers or signs to drive onto a closed road is illegal and carries double penalties for work-zone violations.

teaching.text: Moving barriers or signs to drive onto a closed road is illegal and brings double work-zone penalties. Remember: double penalties apply.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Moving barriers or signs to drive onto a closed road is illegal and carries double penalties for work-zone violations.

question.text: What happens to speeding fines in work zones, and what do the speed sign colors mean?

answer.text: Speeding fines double in work zones; black and white speed limit signs are regulatory, while orange speed limit signs are advisory and suggest slower, safer speeds.

teaching.text: Speeding fines double in work zones; black and white limit signs are the law and orange ones suggest a safer speed. Remember: fines double in zones.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Speeding fines double in work zones; black and white speed limit signs are regulatory, while orange speed limit signs are advisory and suggest slower, safer speeds.

question.text: Which work-zone speed sign is the legal limit?

answer.text: A black and white speed limit sign in a work zone is the legal limit, while an orange one is only an advisory, safer speed.

teaching.text: In a work zone, the black and white speed sign is the legal limit and the orange one is advice. Remember: black and white rules.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A black and white speed limit sign in a work zone is the legal limit, while an orange one is only an advisory, safer speed.

question.text: What should you do whenever you see orange signs?

answer.text: Whenever you see orange signs, slow down, watch for workers and equipment, follow flaggers' instructions and merge carefully and cooperatively.

teaching.text: Orange signs mean slow down, watch for workers and equipment, follow the flaggers and merge cooperatively. Remember: slow, watch, follow flaggers.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Whenever you see orange signs, slow down, watch for workers and equipment, follow flaggers' instructions and merge carefully and cooperatively.

question.text: Why must you be extra alert in work zones at night?

answer.text: Visibility in work zones may be lower, especially at night, so do not drive tired and watch for sleepy drivers; flaggers and pilot cars often control traffic.

teaching.text: Work-zone visibility can drop at night, so do not drive tired, watch for sleepy drivers, and expect flaggers and pilot cars. Remember: tired drivers, low visibility.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Visibility in work zones may be lower, especially at night, so do not drive tired and watch for sleepy drivers; flaggers and pilot cars often control traffic.

question.text: What must you do when approaching a stopped emergency or service vehicle?

answer.text: When approaching a stopped emergency, utility or service vehicle such as a police car, tow truck, NDOT vehicle or garbage truck, slow to a reasonable speed below the posted limit, proceed with caution and be ready to stop (NRS 484B point six zero seven).

teaching.text: For a stopped emergency, utility or service vehicle, slow to a reasonable speed below the limit, go carefully and be ready to stop. Remember: slow below the limit.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When approaching a stopped emergency, utility or service vehicle such as a police car, tow truck, NDOT vehicle or garbage truck, slow to a reasonable speed below the posted limit, proceed with caution and be ready to stop (NRS 484B point six zero seven).

question.text: Which lane should you use when passing a stopped emergency vehicle?

answer.text: When passing such a stopped vehicle, move if possible into a lane not next to the one it occupies, unless road, traffic or weather conditions make that unsafe or impossible.

teaching.text: When passing a stopped emergency vehicle, move into a lane not next to it if you safely can. Remember: move over a lane.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When passing such a stopped vehicle, move if possible into a lane not next to the one it occupies, unless road, traffic or weather conditions make that unsafe or impossible.

question.text: When else does the slow-down duty apply?

teaching.text: The same slow-down duty covers certain vehicles with non-flashing blue lights and anyone repairing a vehicle at the roadside. Remember: blue lights and repairs.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The slow-down duty also applies when approaching a vehicle showing non-flashing blue lights in certain circumstances and when someone is repairing a vehicle.

question.text: May ordinary drivers stop on a shoulder marked for emergency use?

answer.text: Drivers of non-emergency vehicles may not stop on a highway shoulder marked for emergency use.

teaching.text: A shoulder marked for emergency use is not a place for ordinary drivers to stop. Remember: emergency shoulder, no stopping.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Drivers of non-emergency vehicles may not stop on a highway shoulder marked for emergency use.

question.text: Which vehicles may drive on a signed emergency shoulder?

answer.text: Some emergency vehicles may drive on a paved highway shoulder where signs authorize it, including police, fire engines and ambulances, traffic incident management vehicles, tow cars, coroner vehicles and public transit buses (NRS 484B point two one zero).

teaching.text: Where signs allow, police, fire engines, ambulances, incident vehicles, tow cars, coroner vehicles and transit buses may use the shoulder. Remember: emergency vehicles use shoulders.

question.text: When did the emergency shoulder-use rule take effect?

answer.text: The shoulder-use rule for emergency vehicles took effect on January one, two thousand twenty-four.

teaching.text: The emergency shoulder rule took effect on January one, twenty twenty-four. Remember: started at new year.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The shoulder-use rule for emergency vehicles took effect on January one, two thousand twenty-four.

hooks_spoken: Headlights are required from a half hour after sunset to a half hour before sunrise and whenever you cannot see clearly at one thousand feet.
Dim your high beams at least five hundred feet before oncoming traffic and three hundred feet behind a car you follow.

hooks_spoken: Slow down first in bad weather, because slippery stopping distances can be two to ten times longer.
Without ABS, use gentle touch-and-release braking; with ABS, keep firm, continuous pressure.
Studded snow tires are allowed only from October one through April thirty.

hooks_spoken: If brakes fail, pump, use the parking brake and a lower gear; if the gas pedal sticks, go to neutral and brake; never shift into park.
Never use water on a vehicle fire.

hooks_spoken: After a drift onto the shoulder, stay calm and ease back; in a blowout, grip the wheel and ease off the gas without braking.
Never drive through a flooded road, because a few inches of moving water can push a car away.

hooks_spoken: Speeding fines double in work zones, and black and white signs set the legal limit.
Slow below the limit for stopped emergency and service vehicles, and move over a lane when you can.
